title: Ὄνος ⟨νομιζόμενος λέων εἶναι⟩
titleEn: The Donkey Taken for a Lion
part: The Donkey Taken for a Lion (Chambry 279 · Perry 358)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 279 (= Perry 358). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνος δορὰν λέοντος ἐπενδυθεὶς λέων ἐνομίζετο πᾶσιν, καὶ φυγὴ μὲν ἦν ἀνθρώπων, φυγὴ δὲ ποιμνίων.
sentences.tr: Onos doran leontos ependytheis leōn enomizeto pasin, kai phygē men ēn anthrōpōn, phygē de poimniōn.
sentences.l: A donkey, having put a lion's skin on over himself, was held to be a lion by all, and there was a flight of men, and a flight of flocks.
sentences.i: A donkey who had dressed himself in a lion's skin was taken by everyone for a lion, and men fled and flocks fled.
sentences.n: ἐπενδύομαι is to put a garment on over what one is already wearing; the aorist passive form ἐπενδυθείς carries the middle sense, 'having clothed himself'. Greek makes the point twice by repeating the noun φυγή rather than by using a verb, with μέν and δέ holding the two halves apart.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ ἀνέμου πνεύσαντος ἡ δορὰ περιῃρέθη καὶ γυμνὸς ὁ ὄνος ἦν, τότε δὴ πάντες ἐπιδραμόντες ξύλοις καὶ ῥοπάλοις αὐτὸν ἔπαιον.
sentences.tr: Hōs de anemou pneusantos hē dora periēirethē kai gymnos ho onos ēn, tote dē pantes epidramontes xylois kai rhopalois auton epaion.
sentences.l: But when, a wind having blown, the skin was stripped off from about him and the donkey was bare, then indeed all, having run up, kept beating him with sticks and clubs.
sentences.i: But when a wind blew and the skin was stripped away and the donkey stood bare, then everyone ran up and set about beating him with sticks and clubs.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute, ἀνέμου πνεύσαντος, nested inside the ὡς-clause. ἔπαιον is imperfect: the beating went on and on, where an aorist would have said only that it happened.

sentences.t: Ὅτι πένης καὶ ἰδιώτης ὢν μὴ μιμοῦ τὰ τῶν πλουσίων, μή ποτε καταγελασθῇς καὶ κινδυνεύσῃς· τὸ γὰρ ξένον ἀνοίκειον.
sentences.tr: Hoti penēs kai idiōtēs ōn mē mimou ta tōn plousiōn, mē pote katagelasthēis kai kindyneusēis· to gar xenon anoikeion.
sentences.l: That, being poor and a private man, do not imitate the things of the rich, lest ever you be laughed at and come into danger; for what is foreign is not one's own.
sentences.i: The story shows that, being poor and a private man, you should not imitate the ways of the rich, lest you be laughed at and put in danger; for what is not your own is out of keeping.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. What follows the Ὅτι is not a statement but a command addressed to the reader — μὴ μιμοῦ, present imperative — and μή ποτε with the aorist subjunctive gives the fear the imperative guards against. ἰδιώτης is the private person as against those in office or means.
